Serving as the Soviet Union's largely ceremonial head of state from 1919 to 1946 while real power sat with Stalin, this former metalworker had been mayor of Petrograd after the October Revolution — who was he?
Grand Duke Michael Alexandrovich of Russia
In Arthurian legend, this traitorous nephew — later recast as King Arthur's villainous, incestuously conceived son — died alongside him at the Battle of Camlann — who is he?
Mordred: Character in Arthurian legend. Mordred or Modred ( or; Welsh: Medraut or Medrawt) is a major figure in the legend of King Arthur.
The most prosperous king of Ayutthaya's Prasat Thong dynasty handed extraordinary power to a Greek adventurer named Constantine Phaulkon. Which Thai monarch was he?
Narai: 27th monarch of the Ayutthaya Kingdom (1656–1688)
Shared across Jainism, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Sikhism, this state of liberation marks the end of the cycle of rebirth and the extinguishing of worldly passions — what is it?
Nirvana: Liberation from repeated rebirth in saṃsāra.
Four days after D-Day, a Waffen-SS company destroyed this French village and killed 642 civilians in retaliation for Resistance activity, including the death of a captured SS officer — which village?
Oradour-sur-Glane massacre: 1944 mass killing by Nazi German soldiers in France.
This senior Soviet intelligence officer orchestrated Leon Trotsky's assassination in Mexico in 1940 and later ran spy operations targeting the Manhattan Project — who was he?
A protégé of the dictator Sulla, this Roman general and statesman celebrated three triumphs and was elected consul on three separate occasions during the late Republic — who was he?
Pompey: Roman general and statesman (106–48 BC)
R. Budd Dwyer: American politician (1939–1987). Dwyer committed suicide by gunshot during a press conference following his conviction for accepting a bribe in the CTA scandal.
Beginning 1 May 2019 when Naruhito ascended the Chrysanthemum Throne, this current chapter of Japan's imperial calendar takes its name from a phrase meaning 'beautiful harmony' — what is it called?
Reiwa era: Era of Japanese history (2019–present)
Prince Gustaf Adolf, Duke of Västerbotten
Roman Shukhevych: Ukrainian nationalist militant (1907–1950). Shukhevych led some of the Galicia-Volhynia massacres, where tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed.
After losing three presidential bids, this Chilean socialist finally won in 1970 — often called the first Marxist elected president in a liberal democracy in Latin America. Who was he?
Salvador Allende: President of Chile from 1970 to 1973.
Proclaimed in 1931 after King Alfonso XIII's ouster and toppled in 1939 by Franco's Nationalists, which democratic government ruled Spain through the Civil War era?
Second Spanish Republic: Government of Spain, 1931–1939. It was dissolved on 1 April 1939 after surrendering in the Spanish Civil War to the Nationalists rebels led by General Francisco Franco.
The longest-serving chief minister of Madhya Pradesh, this Indian politician later became national Minister of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare in 2024 — who is he?
Holding the grim distinction of being the only British prime minister ever assassinated, this barrister was also the only attorney-general to reach the top job — who was he?
Spencer Perceval: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1809 to 1812.

First emerging among Spanish and North American workers in the 1870s, this labor movement organizes workers by industry and uses strikes and direct action aiming to seize control of the means of production — what's it called?
Elected archon in 493 BC, this populist Athenian politician championed naval expansion, fought at Marathon, and became Athens's leading statesman ahead of the second Persian invasion — who is he?
Themistocles: Athenian politician and general (c. 524–459 BC)

Elected by Ostrogothic nobles in 541 after his two predecessors were killed for trying to surrender to the Romans, this penultimate Gothic king reversed the tide of the Gothic War and recovered nearly all of Italy by 543 — who was he?
Totila: King of the Ostrogoths from 541 to 552.
The only woman ever to serve as chief minister of Rajasthan, this Indian politician also held two Cabinet posts under Atal Bihari Vajpayee — who is she?

Vasundhara Raje: 11th Chief Minister of Rajasthan. Vasundhara Raje Scindia (born 8 March 1953) is an Indian politician, who has held the position of the chief minister of Rajasthan from 2003 to 2008 and 2013 to 2018.
Deeply in debt to Adolf Hitler for loans he'd borrowed, this aristocratic field marshal commanded Germany's army during the Battle of France and the invasions of Yugoslavia and Greece - who was he?
Walther von Brauchitsch: German Commander-in-Chief during World War II (1881–1948)
The first Canadian prime minister to hold a PhD, this Liberal racked up 21 years and 154 days in office across three non-consecutive terms — the longest tenure in the country's history; who is he?
William Lyon Mackenzie King: Canadian prime minister (1874–1950)
Claiming to be Catherine the Great's dead husband Tsar Peter III, this Cossack leader proclaimed an end to serfdom in 1773 and led a massive peasant uprising across the Volga-Ural region. Who was he?
Yemelyan Pugachev: Russian Cossack rebel leader (1742–1775)
Nicknamed 'The Acquitator' for his string of courtroom wins as a criminal defense lawyer, he served as France's Minister of Justice from 2020 to 2024 — who is he?
Éric Dupond-Moretti: French-Italian politician and lawyer (born 1961)
Which one below was born first?
Maria Goeppert Mayer (born 1906) is the earliest of the four. In 1986, the Maria Goeppert Mayer Award for early-career women physicists was established in her honor.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Franz Reichelt (born 1878) is the earliest of the four. The parachute failed to deploy and he plummeted 57 metres (187 ft) to his death.
Which of these four began earliest?
Messerschmitt Bf 109 (founded 1937) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
MUMPS (founded 1966) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Samuel C. C. Ting is a physicist.
Pick the chemist from these four.
What is the atomic number of Lawrencium?
Lawrencium: Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lr (formerly Lw) and atomic number 103.
In what year was Hypatia born?
Hypatia: Not the only fourth century Alexandrian female mathematician, Hypatia was preceded by Pandrosion.
In what year was Bertrand Russell born?
Bertrand Russell: Bertrand Arthur William Russell, 3rd Earl Russell (18 May 1872 – 2 February 1970), was an English philosopher, logician, mathematician, and public intellectual.
In what year was Ümit Özdağ born?
Ümit Özdağ: On 16 November 2020, Özdağ was also dismissed from the Good Party.
In what year did Hans Albert Einstein die?
Hans Albert Einstein: Hans Albert Einstein (May 14, 1904 – July 26, 1973) was a Swiss-American engineer, the second child and first son of physicists Albert Einstein and Mileva Marić.
In what year did John McAfee die?
John McAfee: In 1987, he wrote the first commercial anti-virus software, founding McAfee Associates to sell his creation.
In what year was Special relativity discovered?
Special relativity: In physics, the special theory of relativity, or simply special relativity, is a scientific theory of the relationship between space and time.
In what year was Mustard gas discovered?
Mustard gas: There is no preventive agent against mustard gas, with protection depending entirely on skin and airways protection, and no antidote exists for mustard poisoning.
Sodium acetate: Pfizer. Sodium acetate is a chemical compound with formula CH3COONa, also abbreviated NaOAc.
Which country is Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider from?

Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider: United States. Part of the Long Range Strike Bomber (LRS-B) program, it is to be an intercontinental strategic bomber that can deliver conventional and thermonuclear weapons.
Who is credited with discovering Archaea?
Archaea: Carl Woese. Archaea (ar-KEE-ə) is a domain of organisms.
Who is credited with discovering Synapse?
Synapse: Charles Scott Sherrington. In the nervous system, a synapse is a structure that allows a neuron to exchange (receive or send) signals with another cell in its immediate vicinity.
Who is credited with discovering Nitrogen?
Nitrogen: Daniel Rutherford. Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
Known by the abbreviation NAC, this mucolytic drug treats acetaminophen overdose and also loosens thick mucus in people with chronic lung conditions like pneumonia and bronchitis — which drug?

Acetylcysteine (NAC) is a mucolytic that is used to treat paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and to loosen thick mucus in individuals with chronic bronchopulmonary disorders, such as pneumonia and bronchitis.
Believed to be an autoimmune attack that breaches the immune privilege of hair follicles, this condition typically leaves a few coin-sized bald spots on the scalp — what is it?
Alopecia areata (AA), also known as spot baldness, is a condition in which hair is lost from some or all areas of the body.
A spinoff of The Originals set within a broader vampire-fiction universe, this CW series follows a teenage witch navigating her supernatural legacy. What show is it?
Anteater are the four extant mammal species in the suborder Vermilingua (meaning 'worm tongue'), commonly known for eating ants and termites.
A methyl ester built from aspartic acid and phenylalanine, this non-saccharide sweetener is among the most-studied food additives ever, judged safe by over 100 regulatory bodies — what is it?
Aspartame is an artificial, non-saccharide sweetener commonly used as a sugar substitute in foods and beverages.
Their foliage is almost indistinguishable from a cycad's, but flower-like reproductive organs — some likely insect-pollinated — set these common Mesozoic seed plants apart. Which extinct order?
Bennettitales (also known as cycadeoids) is an extinct order of seed plants that first appeared in the Permian period and became extinct in most areas toward the end of the Cretaceous.
Native to the Mediterranean and also called 'starflower,' this annual herb's seeds are pressed for oil even though the plant carries mild toxic alkaloids — which plant?
Borage (or; Borago officinalis), also known as starflower, is an annual herb in the flowering plant family Boraginaceae native to the Mediterranean region.
Its three-dimensional shape mimics adenosine closely enough to plug into the same receptors, blocking the brain's signal to wind down — which psychoactive substance is it?
Caffeine is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant of the methylxanthine class and is the most commonly consumed psychoactive substance globally.
Mature females are cows, the intact males are bulls, and the castrated males pull plows as oxen — all names for one widespread domesticated bovine kept as livestock. What animal is it?
Cattle (Bos taurus) are large, domesticated, bovid ungulates widely kept as livestock.
Grown for blue-flowered roadside roots that become a coffee substitute, or for bitter salad leaves like escarole and radicchio, which plant genus covers both chicory and endive?
Cichorium is a genus of plants in the tribe Cichorieae within the family Asteraceae.

Often called the most renowned Greek mathematician since antiquity, he spent his career in Germany advancing measure theory and the calculus of variations — and even built an axiomatic formulation of thermodynamics. Who was he?
Constantin Carathéodory (13 September 1873 - 2 February 1950) was a Greek mathematician who spent most of his professional career in Germany.
As of December 2025 worth an estimated $8.7 billion, this Swedish businessman founded and chairs a massive music-streaming company — who is he?
Daniel Ek (Swedish; born 21 February 1983) is a Swedish businessman and technologist.

England-born but raised in Australia, this geologist did much of his real rock-hunting in the Flinders Ranges — though he's better remembered for braving the ice alongside Shackleton on the Nimrod Expedition; who was he?
Douglas Mawson (5 May 1882 - 14 October 1958) was an Australian geologist, Antarctic explorer, and academic.
Psychology, medicine, history, and even computer science all study these pleasure-or-displeasure states, which still lack any agreed scientific definition — what are they?
Emotion are physical and mental states brought on by neurophysiological changes, variously associated with thoughts, feelings, behavioral responses, and a degree of pleasure or displeasure.
This sensory organ detects light and converts it into electro-chemical signals in neurons, using an adjustable lens system to focus incoming light and form images — name the organ?
Eye is a sensory organ that allows an organism to perceive visual information.
Sitting just below caesium as the second-most electropositive element, this alkali metal decays so fast that a bulk sample has never actually been seen — what is it?
Francium is a chemical element; it has symbol Fr and atomic number 87.
Before he founded a piece of the U.S. aircraft industry, this pioneer set an unofficial world speed record astride a V8-powered motorcycle that stood unbroken until 1911. Who was he?
Glenn Curtiss (May 21, 1878 - July 23, 1930) was an American aviation and motorcycling pioneer, and a founder of the U.S.
Named for a flattened, laterally extended head shape called a cephalofoil, with eyes placed at each end of the T, this family of sharks includes species mostly grouped in one genus — which sharks?

Hammerhead shark are a group of sharks that form the family Sphyrnidae, named for the unusual and distinctive form of their heads, which are flattened and laterally extended into a cephalofoil (a T-shape or "hammer").
Domesticated in Central Asia around 4000 BCE, this one-toed hoofed mammal evolved over 45 million years from the small, multi-toed Eohippus — what is it?
Horse (Equus ferus caballus) is a domesticated, one-toed, hoofed mammal.

Co-creator of the breakthrough neural network AlexNet and a contributor to landmark AI systems including GPT and AlphaGo, this computer scientist has won a major deep-learning research award three years running — who is he?
Ilya Sutskever (born 1986) is a computer scientist who specializes in machine learning.

Designed under the philosophy 'write once, run anywhere,' this high-level, memory-safe, object-oriented programming language compiles to bytecode executed by a dedicated virtual machine — name the language?
Java (programming language) is a high-level, general-purpose, memory-safe, object-oriented programming language.
Diagnosed via corneal topography and linked to frequent eye rubbing and allergies, this progressive disorder causes the cornea to bulge into a cone shape — which eye condition?
Keratoconus is an eye disorder in which the cornea, the transparent front part of the eye, gradually thins and bulges outward into a cone shape.
Named for the German city where it was bred in the mid-19th century, this is a large German dog breed — which breed?
Leonberger is a German breed of large dog. The breed name derives from that of the city of Leonberg, in Baden-Württemberg, where it was bred in the mid-nineteenth century.
Reclassified in 2021 as part of the order Psocodea alongside booklice and barklice, these tiny wingless parasites cement their eggs to a single host for life — what are they called?
Louse (pl.: lice) is the common name for any member of the infraorder Phthiraptera, which contains nearly 5,000 species of wingless parasitic insects.
He helped uncover the Antarctic ozone hole and shared a 1995 Nobel for exposing the danger CFCs pose to the ozone layer — which Mexican chemist?
Mario Molina (19 March 1943 - 7 October 2020) was a Mexican physical chemist.

This American theoretical physicist and science communicator, a professor at the City College of New York, won a 2021 lifetime achievement award named for a famous science-fiction author, honoring his work bridging science and sci-fi. Who is he?
Michio Kaku (born January 24, 1947) is an American theoretical physicist, science communicator, futurologist, and writer of popular science.
One of the four basic animal tissue types, this contractile tissue comes in skeletal, cardiac, and smooth forms and relies on the proteins actin and myosin to generate movement — name the tissue?
Muscle is a specialised soft tissue, one of the four basic types of animal tissues.
This nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug treats acute pain and osteoarthritis by blocking prostaglandin production, though it carries a risk of liver side effects. Name the drug?
Nimesulide is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) with pain medication and fever reducing properties.
Triggered by repeated tension on the growth plate of the upper shinbone from running or jumping sports, this condition causes a tender bump below the kneecap in teens — what is it?
Osgood–Schlatter disease (OSD) is inflammation of the patellar ligament at the tibial tuberosity (apophysitis) usually affecting adolescents during growth spurts.
Known in the US as a goober and in the UK as a monkey nut, this Fabaceae crop hides its edible seeds in underground pods. What is it?

Peanut (Arachis hypogaea), also known as the groundnut, goober (US, via Kikongo), goober pea, pindar (US, via Kikongo) or monkey nut (UK), is a legume crop grown mainly for its edible seeds, contained in underground pods.
Whether captured electronically on a sensor or chemically on light-sensitive film, this art and practice of recording light also powers science and manufacturing — think photolithography. What is it?

Photography is the art, application, and practice of creating images by recording light, either electronically by means of an image sensor, or chemically by means of a light-sensitive material such as photographic film.
Part of the critical theory framework and closely tied to critical race theory, this field analyzes history, literature, and discourse shaped by imperial power — what field is it?

Postcolonialism is the academic study of the cultural, political and economic consequences of colonialism and imperialism, focusing on the impact of human control and exploitation of colonized people and their lands.

Picture benzene, but with one CH swapped for a nitrogen: this flammable, weakly alkaline liquid reeks of fish and underpins countless drugs and vitamins, churned out at 20,000 tons a year — what compound is it?
Pyridine is a basic heterocyclic organic compound with the chemical formula C5H5N.
Also known as vitamin B2, this nutrient builds two key coenzymes for energy metabolism and may, taken orally, cut down on migraine headaches in adults — what is it?
Riboflavin is a vitamin found in food and sold as a dietary supplement.
The FAO/WHO Codex standard recognizes 21 species under this common name for small silvery forage fish, distinguished from their larger 'pilchard' cousins mainly by size — what fish is it?
Sardine are common names for various species of small, oily forage fish in the herring suborder Clupeoidei.
Named for its enormous shoe-shaped bill, this grey wading bird of East African swamps was once filed with storks but now sits beside pelicans — and its closest kin is the hamerkop — what is it?
Shoebill (Balaeniceps rex), also known as the whale-headed stork, whalebill, and shoe-billed stork, is a large long-legged wading bird.

Native to China and Vietnam, this invasive planthopper species has spread destructively across the US, feasting on grapevines and stone fruit as well as its preferred invasive host tree — what insect is it?
Spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) is a species of planthopper indigenous to parts of China and Vietnam.

In the nervous system, this structure lets one neuron send or receive signals with a neighboring cell, and comes in both chemical and electrical varieties — the electrical kind linked directly through gap junctions — name this structure?
Synapse is a structure that allows a neuron to exchange (receive or send) signals with another cell in its immediate vicinity.
A European Space Agency astronaut who is also a musician and writer, this Frenchman logged two six-month stints aboard the ISS, the second launched via SpaceX Crew Dragon in 2021 — who is he?
Thomas Pesquet (French; born 27 February 1978, is a French aerospace engineer, pilot, European Space Agency astronaut, actor, musician, and writer.

These simple-looking marine invertebrates prove their kinship to vertebrates as larvae, when they sport a notochord, a dorsal nerve cord, and a post-anal tail — resembling a tiny tadpole. What are they?
Tunicate are marine invertebrates belonging to the subphylum Tunicata.

Manufactured under license by both Goodyear and Brewster during World War II, this American carrier-based fighter aircraft became one of the most capable fighter-bombers of the war and later saw service in Korea — which aircraft?
Vought F4U Corsair is an American fighter aircraft that saw service primarily in World War II and the Korean War.

This Indian Islamic preacher and comparative-religion scholar delivers his speeches in English while wearing a suit and tie, and founded both a research foundation and a television channel called Peace TV — who is he?
Zakir Naik (born 18 October 1965) is an Indian Islamic da'i and orator who focuses on comparative religion.
Prescribed for ADHD and narcolepsy but also misused as a euphoriant, this fixed-dose pill packs four different amphetamine salts into one tablet. What is its brand name?
Adderall: Drug mixture used mainly to treat ADHD and narcolepsy.
This Scottish physician shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for discovering penicillin, and in 1922 identified an enzyme in his own nasal discharge — who is he?
Alexander Fleming: Scottish physician and microbiologist (1881–1955)
This highly soluble, hygroscopic crystalline salt is prized as a high-nitrogen fertilizer but is also the major ingredient in the industrial explosive ANFO — what is it?
Ammonium nitrate: Chemical compound with formula NH4NO3.
This scientific practice of systematically measuring the human body has been used in paleoanthropology, historical living-standards research, and modern clothing design — what is it called?
Anthropometry: Measurement of the human individual.
Known as mugwort or wormwood, this daisy-family plant has long been used for both medicinal and culinary purposes — what species is it?

Artemisia vulgaris: Medicinal plant known as common mugwort. It is one of several species in the genus Artemisia commonly known as mugwort, although Artemisia vulgaris is the species most often called mugwort.
Blooming for weeks each spring and thriving in the shade under trees, these flowering shrubs belong to the genus Rhododendron — what are they called?
Azalea: Subgroup of rhododendron flowering shrubs.
Named after a barberry-related plant genus and glowing bright yellow under ultraviolet light, this alkaloid was recorded in an ancient Chinese herbal medicine text around 200 BC. What compound is it?
This crested songbird in the crow family sports a black, U-shaped collar and is known for hiding acorns to eat later — which eastern North American bird?
Blue jay: Species of bird. The blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata) is a passerine bird in the family Corvidae, native to eastern North America.

Unique among mammals, human females are the only ones to permanently develop this secondary sex organ at puberty rather than just during pregnancy, and it later produces milk via the mammary gland — which body part?
Breast: Part of the female primate torso that has mammary glands.
The fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust and a reactive alkaline earth metal, this element's name comes from the Latin word for 'lime' obtained by heating limestone — what is it?
Calcium: Chemical element with atomic number 20 (Ca)
This compound ferries long-chain fatty acids into a cell's mitochondria to be burned for energy and is naturally concentrated in muscles like the heart — what is it?
Carnitine: Compound active in mitochondria. Carnitine is a quaternary ammonium compound involved in metabolism in most mammals, plants, and some bacteria.
In calculus, this formula computes the derivative of a composite function by multiplying together the derivatives of its two component functions — what is it called?

Native to Sri Lanka, the inner bark of this evergreen tree is the original source of a beloved baking spice, sometimes distinguished from a cheaper cousin as the 'true' or 'Ceylon' variety — which tree?
Cinnamomum verum: Species of tree. The inner bark of the tree is historically regarded as the spice cinnamon, though this term was later generalized to include C. cassia as well.
Named for an Indonesian island where an 18th-century naturalist first catalogued it, this pungent, oregano-scented succulent also goes by Cuban oregano and Indian borage — which plant?
Coleus amboinicus: Species of plant. Coleus amboinicus is a species of semi-succulent perennial plant in the family Lamiaceae.
Produced mainly by the adrenal cortex and surging in response to stress and low blood sugar, this steroid hormone is sold as medicine under the name hydrocortisone — what is it?
Built from microfilaments, intermediate filaments, and microtubules, this network gives a cell its shape and lets it contract and migrate — what is it?
Cytoskeleton: Network of filamentous proteins that forms the internal framework of cells.
Carnations and sweet williams both belong to which flowering plant genus of about 340 species, native mainly to Europe and Asia?
Attracted to rotting fruit and fermenting drinks, this insect became the first animal launched into space in 1946 and has earned six Nobel Prizes for scientists who studied it — what is it?
Drosophila melanogaster: Species of fruit fly.
Native to southern India, this ginger-family plant produces the aromatic seeds used in both sweet and savory cooking — what is it, botanically?
Elettaria cardamomum: Species of flowering plant.
This fibromuscular tube carries food from throat to stomach using peristaltic contractions, and its name traces to Ancient Greek roots meaning roughly 'I carry what I ate.' What is it?
Esophagus: Vertebrate organ through which food passes to the stomach.
Carried out by the lungs, kidneys, and skin in vertebrates, this bodily process rids the body of metabolic byproducts like urea, carbon dioxide, and uric acid — what is it called?
Excretion: Elimination of metabolic waste products by an organism.
Spending 36 years at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory contributing to America's robotic space missions, which Iranian-American scientist later advised high-tech startups after retiring in 2016?
Traditionally pounded from cassava, plantains, and cocoyam, this West African staple gets a shoutout in Chinua Achebe's novel Things Fall Apart — what dish is it?
Fufu: Dough-like food in African cuisine.

Among the longest of all living crocodilians, this fish-eater wields a slender snout lined with 110 interlocking teeth, and the males sport a bulbous, pot-shaped bump on the tip that gives the animal its name. What is it?
Gharial: Crocodilian native to the Indian subcontinent.
This branch of discrete mathematics studies structures made of vertices connected by edges, modeling pairwise relationships between objects — what field is it?

Graph theory: Area of discrete mathematics. In mathematics and computer science, graph theory is the study of graphs, which are mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects.

This prehensile, multi-fingered body part sits at the end of primates' forelimbs — koalas famously have two opposable thumbs on each one, while raccoons are often said to have them despite lacking true opposable thumbs. What is it?
Hand: Extremity at the end of an arm or forelimb.
Named after the 19th-century physicist who proved electromagnetic waves exist, which SI unit measures one cycle per second?
Hertz: SI unit of frequency. The hertz (symbol: Hz) is the unit of frequency in the International System of Units (SI), often described as being equivalent to one event (or cycle) per second.
This condition involves a buildup of cerebrospinal fluid around the brain, causing headaches, vision problems, and in babies a rapidly enlarging head — what is it?
Hydrocephalus: Abnormal increase in cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles of the brain.
Powered by four Aviadvigatel turbofans and built in Voronezh, this Soviet-designed wide-body jet now serves mainly as the Russian president's aircraft — which airliner?
Ilyushin Il-96: Russian four-engined long-range wide-body jet airliner.
Resembling a mustelid despite being a wild cat, this Americas-native feline comes in gray or red color morphs and once roamed as far north as Texas — which species?
Jaguarundi: Species of felid. Its range extends from central Argentina in the south and much of South America east of the Andes, through Central America, and into northern Mexico.
He wrote the first commercial anti-virus software in 1987, then later urged people to uninstall the product bearing his name and twice ran for U.S. president — who was he?
John McAfee: British and American programmer and businessman (1945–2021)
With an average length of 3.18 to 4 meters and a record of 5.85 meters, this snake is the world's longest venomous species, endemic to Asia. What is it?
King cobra: Group of venomous snakes from Asia.

The smallest member of the genus Mustela, this slender carnivore has been introduced to New Zealand, Malta, Crete, the Azores, and São Tomé despite being native across Eurasia and North Africa — what is it?
Element number 3, this soft silvery-white alkali metal is the least dense metal of all and so reactive it must be stored under oil or in an inert atmosphere — what is it?
Lithium: Chemical element with atomic number 3 (Li)
Found in the hundreds inside most animal cells but almost never in plant cells, this acidic, enzyme-packed organelle serves as the cell's degradation center — which organelle?
Lysosome: Cell membrane organelle. A lysosome (/ˈlaɪsəˌsoʊm/) is a membrane-bound organelle that is found in all animal cells (except red blood cells), and rarely in plant cells.
The first Mexican-born scientist to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, this physical chemist shared the 1995 award for revealing how CFC gases threaten the ozone layer — who?
Nicknamed 'meow meow' and chemically related to compounds in the khat plant, this synthetic stimulant produces effects similar to MDMA and was first synthesized in 1929 — which drug?
Mephedrone: Recreational drug. Mephedrone, also known as 4-methylmethcathinone, 4-MMC, or 4-methylephedrone, is a synthetic stimulant drug belonging to the amphetamine and cathinone classes.

Given the NATO reporting name 'Hip,' this Soviet-designed helicopter family has been in continuous production since 1975 as a medium twin-turbine transport, with an armed gunship variant — which aircraft?
Mil Mi-17: Family of Russian military transport helicopters.
Built with a slender segmented body and a long piercing-and-sucking proboscis, this family of 3,600 fly species diversified back in the Cretaceous — what are they?
Mosquito: Family of flies. The word mosquito (formed by mosca and diminutive -ito) is Spanish and Portuguese for little fly.

As modern science emerged, this concept came to mean the passive reality moved by divine laws — and after the Industrial Revolution, the part of the world untouched by intentional human hands. What word is it?
Nature: Material world and its phenomena.
Made from red algae and dried into flat sheets through a process resembling papermaking, this ingredient has wrapped sushi and rice balls in Japan since the 700s — what is it?
Nori: Edible seaweed species of the red algae genus Pyropia.
Its Greek name means 'serpent-bearer,' and it's depicted as a man grasping a snake represented by a neighboring constellation — which constellation straddles the celestial equator?
Ophiuchus: Constellation straddling the celestial equator. Ophiuchus ( o-fee-YOO-kəs) is a large constellation straddling the celestial equator.
This butterfly was the first species to be given the common name now applied to its entire family, and is widespread across the Palearctic and North America — which species?
Papilio machaon: Species of insect. Papilio machaon, the Old World swallowtail, is a butterfly of the family Papilionidae.

This term for 'parts in each thousand' is symbolized by ‰ — a percent sign with an extra zero — and sits right next to the percent sign in Unicode's General Punctuation block — what is this unit called?
Per mille: Unit for parts per thousand. The associated symbol is ‰, similar to a per cent sign % but with an extra zero in the divisor.

Also known as physiography, this branch of natural science studies the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, and geosphere — as opposed to the branch focused on the built human environment. Which field of study?
Physical geography: Study of processes and patterns in the natural environment.

Derived from renewable resources such as corn starch and capable of biodegrading, this thermoplastic polyester made up about a quarter of the world's bioplastic market in 2022 — what compound is this?
This deciduous member of the rose family includes many varieties known as plums in English, with greengages and damsons among its subspecies — which species is it?
Prunus domestica: Species of flowering plant.

Historically nicknamed 'hydrophobia' because sufferers panic at the offer of a drink, this viral disease causes severe brain inflammation and is virtually always fatal once symptoms appear. What is it?
